objectives: Explain how residuals keep gradients flowing
Describe the residual stream as a shared bus

slides.title: Part 1 — Why depth used to be impossible
slides.body: Before 2015, beyond ~20 layers, *adding* layers made networks *worse* — even though a deeper net can represent everything a shallower one can. One architectural trick fixed it and now every deep net uses it.

slides.title: The vanishing/exploding gradient wall
slides.body:
In a deep stack, the loss gradient is multiplied through every layer's weights and nonlinearities on the way back to layer 1. Each multiplication tends to shrink it (vanish) or grow it (explode). By layer 1 the signal is noise.

**Residual connections** (He et al., 2015): add the input directly to the output.

$$y = x + F(x)$$

$F$ is the layer (attention, FFN, conv — anything). The identity path $x$ flows through untouched, giving the gradient a clean route home.

slides.title: The +1 that saves training
slides.body:
Differentiate $y=x+F(x)$:

$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=1+\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}$$

The **+1** is the magic. Even if $\partial F/\partial x$ vanishes or explodes, the sum still has a healthy 1 in it — gradient flows. Over $N$ residual layers the gradient is a product of $(1+\partial F_i/\partial x)$ terms; as long as each stays near 1, the product stays bounded. Result: **arbitrarily deep networks become trainable** (modern transformers are 50–100+ layers).

question.question: What is ∂/∂x of y = x + F(x)?
options: 1 + ∂F/∂x — the +1 from the identity path keeps gradients alive even if ∂F/∂x vanishes
question.explanation: Identity path derivative = 1; F path derivative = ∂F/∂x; sum = 1 + ∂F/∂x. That additive 1 is precisely what prevents vanishing gradients in deep stacks — even a layer that learns nothing still passes the gradient backward unchanged.

question.question: Write a residual layer's output y in terms of input x and the sublayer function F.
question.hint: Add the input to the sublayer's output.
question.explanation: y = x + F(x). The output is NOT just F(x) (that would be a plain layer) and NOT just x (that would skip the layer). It is the sum — F learns a *delta* to add to the running representation.

slides.title: Part 2 — The residual stream
slides.body: The single most useful mental model for how transformer layers compose.

slides.title: A shared bus every layer reads and writes
slides.body:
The **residual stream** is the running sum at each token position as you go up the layers:

```
r0 = embed(token) + position
r1 = r0 + Attention(LN(r0))
r2 = r1 + FFN(LN(r1))
... × L layers ...
logits = unembed(LN(r_2L))
```

Each sublayer **reads** from the stream (via LN), computes an update, and **adds** it back. The activation panel shows how each layer's contribution stacks into this running representation. Mech-interp describes circuits as layers "writing" a signal into the stream and later layers "reading" it back — e.g. an induction circuit.

slides.title: The 'skip connection' misconception
slides.body:
Residuals are often mis-described as "skip connections that let layers be skipped." The layer is **not** skipped — its output is *added*:

```
y = x + F(x)   # NOT just x, NOT just F(x)
```

F's job becomes "learn the *delta* — what to add to the running representation," not "produce the full output." The network as a whole is the *sum of all these learned updates*. That reframing — every layer is an incremental edit to a shared stream — is why deep residual nets work and how interpretability reasons about them.

question.question: In the residual stream, what is a layer L attention sublayer's role?
options: Read from the stream (after LN), compute a per-token update, and add it back
Replace the stream entirely with attention's output
Stop gradient flow at this layer
question.explanation: It reads (LN-preprocessed), computes, and writes additively — augmenting the running representation, never replacing it. This additive-update view is the central abstraction of how transformer layers compose, and why the residual is not mere plumbing.

question.question: Derive why residuals enable depth
question.goal: From: plain deep stacks won't train.

steps.prompt: Why do plain very-deep stacks fail to train?
steps.motivation: Each layer's Jacobian factor <1 multiplies across depth → gradients vanish.

options: Repeated <1 Jacobian factors make gradients vanish with depth

hints: Think product of many small numbers.
steps.reveal: Backprop multiplies per-layer factors; if each <1, deep products → 0.

steps.prompt: Write a residual block output and its derivative wrt x.
steps.motivation: The identity path contributes a +1 to the gradient so it can't vanish.
steps.reveal: y=x+F(x) ⇒ ∂y/∂x = I + F'(x): the I keeps gradient flowing at any depth.

question.prompt: Explain residual connections to your pet: the problem and the one-line fix.

rubricCriteria.description: deep plain nets vanish gradients (product of <1 factors)
the skip path is the identity, adding a +1 to the gradient
this lets very deep networks train

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- $y=x+F(x)$ adds **+1** to the gradient → deep stacks train.
- The **residual stream** is a shared bus every sublayer reads from and adds to.
- Each layer learns a **delta**, not a full replacement (not a 'skip').
- With [layer norm](/wiki/layer-normalization), this is *why* 50–100-layer transformers are possible.

**Next:** assemble attention + FFN + residual + norm into the [transformer block](/wiki/transformer-block) — the unit stacked N times to make a real model.
